title: The risk-neutral measure made rigorous
objectives: Show that discounted prices are martingales under the risk-neutral measure.

screens.title: Discounted prices on the tree
screens.prose: The trees course's tree, with every price discounted to today: $\tilde S_n = S_n/1.05^n$. The pricing chance is $q = 0.625$ and the real up chance is $p = 0.7$. Test whether each node's price is the average of the two after it.
screens.question: Fill in the average at the up node under $q$, and at the root under $p$.

columns: Average of the next two prices

hints.text: The two prices after the up node are £130.61 and £87.07.
Weight them by $0.625$ and $0.375$.
For the root, weight £114.29 and £76.19 by 0.7 and 0.3.

feedback.correct: Under $q$ the up node averages to £114.29, its own price, so $\tilde S$ is a martingale. Under $p = 0.7$ the root averages to £102.86, not £100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the two later prices by the chances on their branches.

byKey.r0c1: Use $0.625 \times 130.61 + 0.375 \times 87.07$. Equal weights give 108.84, and 0.7 gives 117.55.
byKey.r1c1: Use $0.7 \times 114.29 + 0.3 \times 76.19$. With $q$ the root would average to £100.00.

explain.text: $0.625 \times 130.61 + 0.375 \times 87.07 = 114.29$: under $q$ every node is the average of the two after it. Under $p = 0.7$ the root is $0.7 \times 114.29 + 0.3 \times 76.19 = 102.86$, so discounted prices drift up under $P$.

screens.title: Equivalent martingale measures
screens.prose: An **equivalent martingale measure** is a $Q$, equivalent to $P$, with every discounted price a martingale under it. The **fundamental theorem of asset pricing** says: no arbitrage exactly when one exists, completeness exactly when it is unique. Harrison and Pliska proved it on finite markets; Dalang, Morton and Willinger extended it.
screens.question: Which statement is the fundamental theorem on a finite tree?

options.text: No arbitrage exactly when some equivalent $Q$ makes discounted prices martingales
No arbitrage exactly when $P$ itself makes discounted prices martingales
options.why: You used $P$. The root drifted to £102.86 under $P$ and there is still no arbitrage: only some $Q$ is needed.

options.text: No arbitrage exactly when $q$ equals the real up chance $p$
options.why: You equated $Q$ with $P$. Here $q = 0.625$ and $p = 0.7$ differ, and the tree is arbitrage-free.

options.text: Complete exactly when an equivalent martingale measure exists
options.why: You merged two properties. Existence gives no arbitrage; with no arbitrage, uniqueness gives completeness.

hints.text: The theorem links an economic property to the existence of a measure.
Which measure? $P$ drifted at the root; the pricing chance $q$ did not.
A measure equivalent to $P$ is enough.

feedback.correct: No arbitrage exactly when an equivalent martingale measure exists; complete exactly when it is unique.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide which of $P$ or some $Q$ must make the prices martingales.

byKey.b: $P$ is not required to remove the drift. $Q$ does.
byKey.c: $q$ and $p$ may differ. Equivalence only asks them to share null sets.
byKey.d: Existence is no arbitrage; uniqueness is completeness.

explain.text: On the tree, $Q$ with $q = 0.625$ exists and is unique: no arbitrage, and the market is complete. Harrison and Pliska prove both parts for finite markets; in continuous time a martingale measure still rules out arbitrage (Shreve II, section 5.4), but the converse needs a stronger condition than no arbitrage. Equivalence is what lets arguments move between $P$ and $Q$.

screens.title: When no q exists
screens.prose: One period: $q = \tfrac{1 + r - d}{u - d}$, which lies in $(0, 1)$ exactly when $d < 1 + r < u$. Now let the up factor be $u = 1.04$, with $d = 0.8$ and $r = 5\%$.
screens.question: Compute $q$ to four decimal places.

hints.text: The numerator is 0.25 and the denominator is 0.24.

feedback.correct: $q = \tfrac{0.25}{0.24} = 1.0417$, above 1. No equivalent martingale measure exists, so there is an arbitrage. Short the share and deposit £100 at 5%: you hold £105 and owe at most £104.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $q = (1 + r - d)/(u - d)$.

byKey.old: You used $u = 1.2$ from the earlier tree. This tree has $u = 1.04$.
byKey.complement: You gave $1 - q$. The question asks for $q$ itself, which is above 1.

explain.text: $q = \tfrac{1.05 - 0.8}{1.04 - 0.8} = \tfrac{25}{24} = 1.0417 > 1$, so $1 + r = 1.05$ is above $u = 1.04$: cash beats the share even in the good state. Shorting the share and depositing £100 earns a sure £1 or more. A $q$ outside $(0, 1)$ signals an arbitrage.

screens.title: The easy direction, proved
screens.prose: Let $Q$ be an equivalent martingale measure. We show no strategy has $V_0 = 0$, $V_N \ge 0$ and $P(V_N > 0) > 0$. Write $\tilde V_n$ for discounted value and $\Delta_k$ for the shares held over step $k$. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order, a reason in each line. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: A self-financing strategy has $\tilde V_n = V_0 + \sum_{k \le n}\Delta_k(\tilde S_k - \tilde S_{k-1})$ with $\Delta_k$ predictable, because cash earns exactly the discount rate.
Under $Q$ this is a martingale transform of $\tilde S$ (lesson 12), so $\tilde V$ is a $Q$-martingale and $E_Q[\tilde V_N] = V_0 = 0$.
With $V_N \ge 0$ we have $\tilde V_N \ge 0$ and $E_Q[\tilde V_N] = 0$, so $Q(V_N > 0) = 0$.
$Q$ is equivalent to $P$, so $P(V_N > 0) = 0$ as well: no arbitrage. $\blacksquare$
Since $P(V_N > 0) > 0$, $E_P[\tilde V_N] > 0$, which contradicts the martingale property.
lines.why: You used the wrong measure. $\tilde V$ is a martingale under $Q$, and a positive $P$-chance must be carried to $Q$ by equivalence.

lines.text: $Q$ is the real-world measure, so $\tilde V$ is also a $P$-martingale.
lines.why: You identified $Q$ with $P$. Under $P$ the discounted price drifts up: £102.86 at the root against £100.

hints.text: Write the strategy's discounted value as a sum of gains on the share.
A martingale transform of a martingale is a martingale.
Order: gains formula, martingale, zero chance under $Q$, zero chance under $P$.

feedback.correct: Right. The martingale gives $E_Q[\tilde V_N] = 0$. A non-negative variable with mean 0 is 0 almost surely, and equivalence carries that to $P$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Gains formula, martingale transform, then move from $Q$ to $P$ by equivalence.

byKey.d1: You used $P$ for the martingale step. The transform argument works under $Q$.
byKey.d2: You treated $Q$ as the real world. They differ, and the proof needs both.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: The martingale transform makes $\tilde V$ a $Q$-martingale, so $E_Q[\tilde V_N] = 0$. A non-negative variable with mean 0 is 0 with $Q$-chance 1. Equivalence passes that to $P$: no arbitrage, which is the easy half of the theorem.

screens.title: Pricing by the martingale
screens.prose: A replicating portfolio's discounted value is a $Q$-martingale, so its cost today is $V_0 = E_Q[\text{payoff}]/1.05^2$. Price the put struck at £100 on the two-step tree ($q = 0.625$). It pays £0, £4 and £36 at the year-2 nodes.
screens.question: What is the put worth today?

hints.text: The $Q$-chances of UU, UD or DU, and DD are 0.390625, 0.46875 and 0.140625.
Only the middle and bottom nodes pay: $0.46875 \times 4 + 0.140625 \times 36$.
Discount twice: divide by $1.05^2 = 1.1025$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{1.875 + 5.0625}{1.1025} = \text{£}6.29$, the put price of trees lesson 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight by $q$ chances, then discount twice.

byKey.onedisc: You discounted once. The payoff comes after two steps, so divide by $1.05^2$.
byKey.real: You used the real chance 0.7. Pricing uses $q$.

explain.text: $E_Q[\text{payoff}] = 0.46875 \times 4 + 0.140625 \times 36 = 6.9375$, and $6.9375/1.1025 = \text{£}6.29$. Put-call parity checks it: £15.59 $-$ £6.29 $= \text{£}9.30 = 100 - 100/1.1025$. The discounted value of the replicating portfolio is a $Q$-martingale, so no other price is arbitrage-free.

screens.title: The same fact in continuous time
screens.prose: Under the $Q$ of ito lesson 10 and lesson 16, $dS_t = rS_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,d\tilde W_t$. The picture shows the mean of the discounted price $e^{-rt}S_t$ under $P$ and under $Q$, with $\mu = 12\%$ and $r = 5\%$.
screens.question: What is the $dt$ term of $d(e^{-rt}S_t)$ under $Q$?

options.text: No $dt$ term: only $\sigma e^{-rt}S_t\,d\tilde W_t$ is left
$(\mu - r)e^{-rt}S_t\,dt$, the excess return that remains
options.why: You used the drift under $P$. Under $Q$ the share drifts at $r$, and $\mu$ has gone.

options.text: $r\,e^{-rt}S_t\,dt$, the share's drift under $Q$ that remains
options.why: You kept the share's drift under $Q$ and forgot to subtract the discount. The product rule adds $-re^{-rt}S_t\,dt$.

options.text: $-r\,e^{-rt}S_t\,dt$, the discount's own drift that remains
options.why: You kept the discount's $-r$ and dropped the share's $+r$ under $Q$. The two cancel.

hints.text: Use the product rule on $e^{-rt}$ and $S_t$.
The discount contributes $-re^{-rt}S_t\,dt$ and the share contributes $+re^{-rt}S_t\,dt$ under $Q$.
They cancel.

feedback.correct: The $dt$ terms cancel, so $e^{-rt}S_t$ is a $Q$-martingale: $E_Q[e^{-rT}S_T] = S_0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the discount's $-r$ and the share's drift under $Q$.

byKey.b: $\mu - r$ is the excess return under $P$. Under $Q$, $\mu$ is replaced by $r$.
byKey.c: The share grows at $r$ but the discount factor shrinks at $r$.
byKey.d: The share's drift under $Q$ is $+r$, which cancels the discount.

explain.text: $d(e^{-rt}S_t) = -re^{-rt}S_t\,dt + e^{-rt}(rS_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,d\tilde W_t) = \sigma e^{-rt}S_t\,d\tilde W_t$. With no $dt$ term, $E_Q[e^{-rT}S_T] = S_0$ and the call is $E_Q[e^{-rT}(S_T - K)^+] = \text{£}10.4506$. Under $P$ the mean rises at $\mu - r = 7\%$ a year.

screens.title: Pricing with the real-world chance
screens.prose: A colleague prices the two-step call with her model's up chance $p = 0.7$. She weights the £44 payoff by $0.7^2$ and discounts twice. She says the real chance is what the market believes.
screens.question: What is the call worth, by replication?

hints.text: Replication fixes the price from the tree's prices and the rate alone.
Weight the £44 by $q^2$, not $p^2$.

feedback.correct: £15.59: $q^2 \times 44/1.05^2$. Her price, $0.7^2 \times 44/1.05^2 = \text{£}19.56$, is £3.97 too high: sell her the call and hedge it for £15.59.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price with the pricing chance $q = 0.625$.

byKey.real: You weighted with $p = 0.7$. Replication needs only $u$, $d$ and $r$, so $q$ prices the call and the real chance does not enter.
byKey.onedisc: You discounted once. Two steps need $1.05^2$.

explain.text: The replicating portfolio costs £15.59, whatever $p$ is. At £19.56 you would sell the call, buy the hedge for £15.59 and keep £3.97 for sure. The real chance does not enter: $Q$ is a pricing device, not a belief about investors.

screens.title: An incomplete market
screens.prose: A one-step market has three outcomes: £100 goes to £120, £100 or £80, with $r = 0$. A martingale measure needs $120q_u + 100q_m + 80q_d = 100$ with $q_u + q_m + q_d = 1$ and every $q > 0$. These force $q_u = q_d$.
screens.question: The call struck at £100 costs $20q_u$. Every martingale measure prices it below what number?

hints.text: With $q_u = q_d$, the three chances are $q_u$, $1 - 2q_u$ and $q_u$.
The middle chance $1 - 2q_u$ must be positive.
So $q_u < \tfrac12$ and the price $20q_u < 10$.

feedback.correct: Prices fill the open range £0 to £10: any $q_u$ in $(0, \tfrac12)$ is a martingale measure. The market is incomplete, so no-arbitrage does not fix the price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $q_u = q_d$ and $q_m = 1 - 2q_u > 0$.

byKey.all: You put all the chance on up, $q_u = 1$. Then $q_d = 1$ too, and the chances add to more than 1.
byKey.equal: You took equal chances $\tfrac13$, one martingale measure with price £6.67. Others price higher, up to but never reaching £10.

explain.text: The mean condition gives $20q_u = 20q_d$, so $q_u = q_d = x$ and $q_m = 1 - 2x$. Every $x$ in $(0, \tfrac12)$ is a martingale measure, so the call can cost anything strictly between £0 and £10. The market is incomplete: the theorem finds many $Q$, not one.

screens.title: The tree in code
screens.prose: Prices are exact `Fraction`s. Write `risk_neutral_q(u, d, r)`, which raises `ValueError` when no $q$ in $(0, 1)$ exists. Then write `tree_price` by the binomial expectation, and `is_discounted_martingale`, which checks every node.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction
from math import comb

def risk_neutral_q(u, d, r):
    """q = (1 + r - d) / (u - d), exactly. Raise ValueError unless 0 < q < 1."""
    ...

def tree_price(payoff, S0, u, d, r, n):
    """Price of payoff(S_n) on an n-step recombining tree: E_Q[payoff]/(1 + r)^n, exact."""
    ...

def is_discounted_martingale(S0, u, d, r, p, n):
    """True when, at every node before step n, p * (up price) + (1 - p) * (down price)
    equals the node's price, with prices discounted to time 0."""
    ...
widget.prelude:
from fractions import Fraction
call = lambda s: max(s - 100, 0)
put = lambda s: max(100 - s, 0)
u, d, r = Fraction(6, 5), Fraction(4, 5), Fraction(1, 20)

tests.call: tree_price(lambda s: s, 100, u, d, r, 3)

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests with exact fractions. `call`, `put`, `u`, `d` and `r` are already defined; `comb` is imported. The two-step call gives 15.5896 to four places.

hints.text: Compute $q$ first, then raise `ValueError` if it is not strictly between 0 and 1.
Sum `comb(n, k) * q**k * (1 - q)**(n - k) * payoff(S0 * u**k * d**(n - k))` and divide by $(1 + r)^n$.
For each node $(t, k)$ compare the discounted prices one step later.

feedback.correct: All 12 tests pass. The one-step call is £11.9048 and the two-step call £15.5896. A tree with $u = 1.04$ is refused, and discounted prices are a martingale at $p = 0.625$ but not at 0.7.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every value a `Fraction` and test $0 < q < 1$ exactly.

explain.text: `risk_neutral_q` refuses a tree with an arbitrage. `tree_price` is the binomial expectation under $Q$, discounted once at $(1 + r)^n$. `is_discounted_martingale` returns `True` only when $pu + (1 - p)d = 1 + r$, that is when $p = q$.

screens.title: The interview question
screens.prose: An interviewer asks: why is the discounted price a martingale under $Q$? The table sets $P$ and $Q$ side by side for our tree.
screens.question: Which answer is right?

options.text: Otherwise there is an arbitrage: a $Q$ equivalent to $P$ exists exactly when there is none
Because investors are risk-neutral, so they price at expected value and ignore risk
options.why: You read $Q$ as a belief. Investors may hate risk; $Q$ is a pricing device that falls out of hedging.

options.text: Because the real-world drift of the share equals $r$, so $P$ and $Q$ coincide
options.why: You assumed $\mu = r$. In our tree $p = 0.7$ gives a drift above $r$, and the price is still £15.59.

options.text: Because $Q$ is the best forecast of the share price, better than any other measure
options.why: You treated $Q$ as a forecast. Forecasts use $P$; $Q$ reweights paths to price.

hints.text: Think about what the fundamental theorem says about $Q$ and arbitrage.
Why must the price of a hedgeable claim not depend on investors' attitudes to risk?
A martingale measure exists because no arbitrage does.

feedback.correct: The discounted price is a $Q$-martingale because $Q$ exists exactly when there is no arbitrage. Nobody needs to be risk-neutral.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name the theorem that links $Q$ to arbitrage.

byKey.b: Risk-neutral names the weights, not the investors.
byKey.c: $\mu = r$ is not needed: the change of measure replaces $\mu$ by $r$.
byKey.d: $Q$ is for pricing. Use $P$ to forecast.

explain.text: The fundamental theorem makes the martingale property a consequence of no arbitrage. In practice jumps and stochastic volatility make markets incomplete. Then many $Q$ exist, and the desk picks one by calibrating to traded option prices.

ideas: An equivalent martingale measure makes every discounted price a martingale. A finite tree has no arbitrage exactly when one exists. With no arbitrage, it is complete exactly when the measure is unique.
Easy direction: a strategy's discounted value is a martingale transform, so a $Q$-martingale. $E_Q[\tilde V_N] = 0$ with $V_N \ge 0$ forces $V_N = 0$ under $Q$, hence under $P$.
Price $= E_Q[\text{payoff}]/(1 + r)^n$: £15.59 for the two-step call, £10.4506 in continuous time. The real chance gives £19.56. An incomplete market gives a range, £0 to £10 for the trinomial call.

formula.name: Risk-neutral price
formula.note: Here $q = \tfrac{1 + r - d}{u - d}$ must lie in $(0, 1)$. Further reading: Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance II, section 5.4 (the fundamental theorems of asset pricing).

summary.trap: The real-world chance does not price the option. $Q$ is a pricing device, not a belief that investors are risk-neutral.

quiz.prose: A tree has $u = 1.1$, $d = 0.95$ and $r = 2\%$ a step.
quiz.question: What is $q$, to four decimal places?

feedback.correct: $q = \tfrac{1.02 - 0.95}{1.1 - 0.95} = 0.4667$, inside $(0, 1)$, so there is no arbitrage.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $q = (1 + r - d)/(u - d)$.

byKey.down: You gave $1 - q$, the down weight. $q$ is the up weight.

quiz.prose: A tree has $u = 1.04$, $d = 0.8$ and $r = 5\%$ a year, so $q = 1.0417$.
quiz.question: Which strategy is an arbitrage?

options.text: Short the share and deposit £100: you hold £105 and owe at most £104
Buy the share with £100 borrowed at 5%: you owe £105 and the share is worth at most £104
options.why: You went long the share. It is worth at most £104 against £105 owed, so you lose in both states.

options.text: None: $q > 1$ is an unusually high chance, not a signal
options.why: You read $q$ as a chance. A value above 1 is not a probability, so no martingale measure exists.

options.text: Buy the share and sell it back at £80
options.why: You described a loss. The down state loses £20.

feedback.correct: Cash grows to £105 while the share is at most £104. Shorting the share is a sure profit of at least £1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the cash's growth with the share's best case.

explain.text: Shorting the share and depositing £100 leaves £105 against at most £104 owed. That is a sure gain of £1 to £25. This is why $1 + r < u$ must hold.

quiz.prose: The course option has $S_0 = K = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$ and $T = 1$. The real drift is 12%. We have $\Phi(0.35) = 0.636831$ and $\Phi(0.15) = 0.559618$.
quiz.question: What is $E_Q[e^{-rT}(S_T - K)^+]$, in £ to four decimal places?

byKey.p: You used the real drift in place of $r$. Under $Q$ the share drifts at $r$ and the call is £10.4506.
byKey.undisc: You forgot to discount the average payoff.

explain.text: $S_0\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2) = 63.6831 - 95.1229 \times 0.559618 = \text{£}10.4506$. This is $E_Q[e^{-rT}(S_T - K)^+]$, the price a simulation under $Q$ estimates and trees with ever more steps approach.

quiz.prose: A one-step market has three outcomes and two traded assets, cash and a share. From £100 the share goes to £120, £100 or £80, with $r = 0$.
quiz.question: What does the fundamental theorem say about the call's price?

options.text: Many martingale measures exist, so no-arbitrage gives only a range of prices
Exactly one martingale measure exists, so the price is unique and the market is complete
options.why: You assumed completeness. Three outcomes and two assets leave one free chance, so there are many measures.

options.text: No martingale measure exists, so there is an arbitrage in this market
options.why: You mixed up the two parts. A measure does exist here: $q_u = q_d$ with any $q_u$ in $(0, \tfrac12)$.

options.text: The price is the $P$-expectation, whatever $Q$ is, since $P$ is the real chance
options.why: You used the real-world chance. Prices are bounded by the martingale measures, not by $P$.

feedback.correct: Incomplete: many $Q$, a range of prices, and the desk calibrates to pick one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the martingale measures.

explain.text: Three outcomes with two assets leave one degree of freedom, so the martingale measures form an interval. The price of a call struck at £100 ranges over (£0, £10).
